name: Chin tuck trainer
lead: A chin tuck trainer is a device, commonly an inflatable pad, strap or resistance band, that provides feedback or load during chin-tuck exercises, also known as craniocervical flexion or neck retraction. The exercise draws the head back over the shoulders by engaging the deep neck flexors and stretching the short extensors at the base of the skull. In appearance communities it is used to address forward head posture, which people associate with a protruding chin, a softer neck-to-chin angle and a weaker-looking jawline in profile photographs.

The look people seek is a head stacked over the shoulders: ear in line with the shoulder, chin drawn back and the jaw-neck line visibly sharper from the side. Practitioners describe the route as a chain: a feedback or resistance aid keeps the movement consistent, the deep neck flexors get stronger, the head sits further back day to day, and profile photographs show a cleaner line. Chin tucks can also be performed with no equipment, and the device is commonly described as a convenience.

Forward head posture, sometimes called text neck, tech neck or nerd neck, is commonly assessed by the craniovertebral angle, with values below about 50 degrees treated as indicating the posture.[1] Meta-analyses of therapeutic exercise for forward head posture report changes in the craniovertebral angle, with more variable effects on pain.[2][3] These reviews concern exercise programmes in general, not trainer devices specifically.

angle.text: People use chin tuck trainers to practise pulling the head back over the shoulders, aiming for a cleaner neck-to-chin angle in profile. Exercise studies measure craniovertebral angle rather than facial appearance.

paras: Chin tuck trainers are small and inexpensive. One common form is an inflatable pad placed between the chin and chest or behind the head, against which the user tucks to hold a position. Another form is a strap or band that creates resistance against the chin or head. Posture braces and screen stands are sold in the same category of posture aids.[1]

A related use of the same movement, chin tuck against resistance (CTAR), employs a ball or device under the chin and is studied in speech and swallowing rehabilitation, which is a separate clinical context from posture.[4][5]

Wikipedia describes forward head posture as a head sitting forward of the shoulders, with the earlobe in front of a vertical line through the shoulder point and the chin poked forward; when marked, the back of the skull can sit ahead of the breastbone.[15] The craniovertebral angle runs from a horizontal line through the seventh cervical vertebra to a line from the ear tragus to that vertebra. According to a Grokipedia article, values under 50 degrees indicate the posture, with 30 to 50 mild and under 30 severe.[1]

Wikipedia attributes a rise in neck and upper back pain in the decade before 2016 to heavy use of laptops, phones and tablets, and lists occupations such as dentists, surgeons, hairdressers and computer workers with long hunched hours.[15] It cites a 2014 estimate by Kenneth Hansraj that a head tilted forward adds roughly 10 pounds of effective load on the neck per inch, and a 2012 Finnish study in which more than two hours a day of computer use in adolescents was associated with more musculoskeletal pain.[15]

A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 cross-sectional studies found a significant difference in head posture between adults with and without neck pain but not in adolescents.[9] A 2022 systematic review examined relationships between forward head posture, postural control and gait.[19]

According to a Grokipedia article on forward head posture, the posture involves a forward translation of the head with shortening and overactivity of the suboccipital muscles, the sternocleidomastoid and upper trapezius, alongside weakness of deep flexors such as the longus colli and capitis.[1] Wikipedia's account likewise describes weak deep neck flexors in a head-forward position and recommends strengthening them, strengthening the mid-back and scapular retractors, and stretching the tight upper trapezius.[15]

Chin-tuck exercise is intended to activate the deep flexors and retract the head. The device supplies feedback about position or adds resistance. A 2018 systematic review covers deep cervical flexor training and physiological functions in chronic neck pain.[18]

A 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Manipulative and Physiological Therapeutics included seven randomised trials with 627 participants with forward head posture. It reported significant pooled effects of corrective exercise on craniovertebral angle and on pain, no significant effect on cranial angle, and graded the evidence for changing craniovertebral angle as strong and the evidence for pain as moderate.[2] A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders examined therapeutic exercises for forward head posture, rounded shoulders and hyperkyphosis in upper crossed syndrome across 22 studies.[3]

Randomised trials have tested added components. A 2022 trial examined adding scapular stabilisation to postural correction exercises in symptomatic forward head posture,[6] a 2024 trial of 60 participants evaluated a postural correction programme with scapular stabilisation and kinesiotaping on craniovertebral angle, scapular position and grip strength,[7] a 2017 trial compared upper thoracic mobilisation with upper cervical mobilisation and stabilisation exercises,[8] a 2024 trial compared neck stabilisation with dynamic exercises in nonspecific neck pain with forward head posture,[17] and a 2024 trial tested eyeball exercise and cervical stabilisation programmes.[20] These exercise-programme studies do not isolate the contribution of a trainer device, and posture changes with exercise are described as requiring repeated practice.

Proponents describe a more projected chin and cleaner neck line after correcting head position. A Grokipedia article states that such changes are postural and soft-tissue related and do not change adult bone structure such as mandibular ramus length or angle.[1] The cited research concerns pain and function and does not measure facial appearance. No published trial found evaluates whether correcting forward head posture changes the apparent jawline or chin.

General descriptions of the exercise say to sit or stand tall with eyes forward and draw the chin straight back, as if making a double chin, without tilting the head down; wall-supported and lying versions are also described.[1] The same Grokipedia article lists posture braces, which reviews report change craniovertebral angle by a few degrees in combination with exercise, and raising screens to eye level among aids.[1] Individuals with neck injury, disc problems or dizziness are generally advised to seek clinical guidance before starting.

Chin-tuck exercise is generally considered low-risk, but repeated or forceful tucks can produce neck muscle soreness or headache in some people. A 2022 review discusses relationships among suboccipital muscles, forward head posture and cervicogenic dizziness.[10] Forum posters raise the possibility of overdoing the movement, discussed below.

In posture and jawline discussions, chin tucks are presented as a free exercise that improves the neck-to-chin angle, and trainers are presented as aids for feedback or load. Members on looksmax.org ask what the purpose of a chin tuck is, whether posture matters for profile and how models and actors pose.[21][12] Because the movement can be performed without equipment, the device is commonly described in comparisons as a convenience rather than a requirement.

Chin tucks also appear in discussion of Mike Mew's orthotropics. Wikipedia describes mewing, the tongue-posture technique developed by John Mew and his son Mike, as an unproven form of oral posture training that gained wide attention on social media, especially in looksmaxxing communities after 2019; the article does not mention chin tucks.[16] A looksmax.org poster links chin tucks to Mike Mew.[11]

No studies found testing chin tuck trainer devices for appearance. Related research includes meta-analyses of therapeutic exercise for forward head posture,[2][3] randomised trials of postural correction programmes,[6][7][8][17][20] a systematic review of the link between forward head posture and neck pain,[9] and systematic reviews of chin tuck against resistance for swallowing rehabilitation after stroke, a different clinical use.[4][5]

In the swallowing literature, a 2022 meta-analysis of nine studies with 548 stroke survivors found that chin tuck against resistance improved swallowing safety and oral intake compared with no exercise.[5]

timeline.event: First laptop produced; Wikipedia links later portable-device use to rising neck and upper back pain.[15]
A composite review by Fejer and colleagues reports adult neck pain point prevalence of 5.9 to 22.2 percent.[15]
The iPhone popularises smartphones; the iPad follows in 2010.[15]
A Finnish study associates more than two hours a day of computer use with musculoskeletal pain in adolescents.[15]
Hansraj publishes an estimate of added neck load from forward head tilt.[15]
Meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (627 participants) reports exercise changes craniovertebral angle in forward head posture.[2]
Meta-analysis of 15 cross-sectional studies finds a head posture difference in adults with neck pain but not adolescents; mewing gains wide social-media attention.[9][16]
Meta-analysis of nine studies finds chin tuck against resistance helps post-stroke swallowing.[5]
Meta-analysis of therapeutic exercises for upper crossed syndrome (22 studies) published; trials of postural programmes with scapular stabilisation.[3][7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, chin tucks and forward head posture are discussed both as a free way to improve profile appearance and as a possible source of problems, with some members questioning whether correction matters or helps. [11][12][13]

claims.claim: The McKenzie chin tuck can cause neck hyperflexion and damage the spine, discs and occipital muscles.
claims.believers: An original poster on looksmax.org argues that the chin tuck promoted by Mike Mew rotates the head into hyperflexion and, if held for long periods, could damage discs and cranio-cervical muscles; a reply in the thread calls this fear mongering and says chin tucks combined with face pulls strengthen the occipital region. [11]
claims.experts: A review of therapeutic exercise reports effects on craniovertebral angle and pain, and chin-tuck exercise is generally described as low-risk, with muscle soreness or headache in some people and guidance to seek clinical advice with neck injury, disc problems or dizziness. [2][10] None of the cited studies examined injury from prolonged or forceful chin tucks.

claims.claim: Forward head posture is common among models and actors, so correcting it may be unnecessary.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster notes that many models and actors have forward head posture and asks whether correcting it is a cope; a reply says they may pose differently for photographs than they walk day to day. [12]
claims.experts: A 2019 review describes forward head posture as the most common cervical postural fault, found at different severities in almost all populations. [9] No study cited here evaluates how head posture affects perceived attractiveness.

claims.claim: Forward head posture during adolescence may contribute to maxillary forward growth.
claims.believers: A reply in a looksmax.org thread says the member had forward head posture through their teens from heavy gaming and has a forward-grown maxilla that other family members lack, and wonders whether the two are related. [12]
claims.experts: No study cited in this article examines a link between head posture and maxillary growth; the cited reviews address craniovertebral angle, pain and function. [2][3][9]

claims.claim: Forward head posture causes many problems throughout the body, and correct posture becomes natural with practice.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread cites an article on forward head posture and says it affects the whole body rather than just the face; one reply says good head posture 'becomes natural' after a while. [13]
claims.experts: A 2019 meta-analysis of cross-sectional studies found a head-posture difference between adults with and without neck pain but not in adolescents, and the authors describe the relationship as controversial. [9] A 2018 meta-analysis reported significant pooled effects of corrective exercise on craniovertebral angle and pain. [2] Posture change is described as needing repeated practice.

claims.claim: Fixing forward head posture can make the face look more recessed.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread title states that fixing forward head posture will make a person look more recessed in profile. [14]
claims.experts: No study cited here evaluates whether correcting forward head posture changes the apparent jawline, chin or profile. [9]

claims.claim: A chin tuck trainer works better than doing chin tucks without equipment.
claims.believers: Sellers and posters present pads and bands as giving feedback and load that make the movement more precise.[21]
claims.experts: No published trial isolates a trainer device; the exercise evidence concerns programmes performed with or without equipment.[2][3]
